raw_case_text:
A previously healthy 60-year-old man from Jiangxi province in China, was admitted to the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University with a 3-day history of fever and convulsions. The patient initially presented with sudden onset of fever and chills, with a maximum temperature of 40 C. Symptomatic treatment with over-the-counter cold medication did not result in improvement. On the second day of illness, the patient developed recurrent generalized seizures accompanied by vomiting of gastric contents, followed by progressive disturbance of consciousness. He had no past medical history, took no regular medications, and had no known drug allergies. He had no history of psychiatric illness and no family history of psychiatric disorders. He was a farmer living in a rural area and had no formal employment.
On admission, his vital signs were as follows: Respiratory rate of 20 breaths per minute, regular heart rate of 76 beats per minute, the patient was febrile with a temperature reading of 37.2 C and a blood pressure of 131/76 mmHg. His chest was clear anteriorly. Neurological examination revealed increased muscle tone and mild neck stiffness, but both Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs were negative.
Laboratory investigations on admission showed a markedly elevated procalcitonin level of 27.68 [0-0.05] ng/mL, heparin-binding protein of 75 [0-15] ng/mL and C- reactive protein level of 69.45 [0-8] mg/L. The white blood cell count was 6.46 x 109/L and the platelet count was decreased at 87 x 109/L. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a white blood cell count of 1 [0-10] /microL, protein levels of 1038 [150-450] mg/L, and glucose levels of 3.18 [2.8-4.4] mmol/L. Liver and kidney function tests revealed elevated alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of 128.7 [9-50] U/L and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 115.2 [15-40] U/L, with a serum creatinine level of 101.8 [57-97] micromol/L. The COVID-19 reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction test was negative.
Chest computed tomography (CT) revealed diffuse ground-glass opacities and patchy consolidations in both lungs (Fig. 1). Brain magnetic resonance (MRI) showed multiple, mildly asymmetric lesions with slightly prolonged T1 and T2 signals involving the bilateral parietal lobes, centrum semiovale, bilateral thalami, brainstem, and bilateral cerebellum. The lesions appeared slightly hyperintense on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and hyperintense on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), with no significant enhancement on post-contrast images (Fig. 2). The imaging findings were considered most consistent with inflammatory lesions.
Cerebrospinal fluid Metagenomic Next-generation Sequencing (mNGS) confirmed leptospiral infection. Empirical antibiotics were adjusted from intravenous vancomycin (1000 mg q12h) and intravenous meropenem (1000 mg q8h) to definitive penicillin sodium (40 WU q8h). The patient achieved marked clinical improvement within two weeks, with follow-up MRI showing a significant reduction of the CNS lesions and chest CT revealing marked resolution of pulmonary infiltrates (Fig. 3, Fig. 4). Approximately three years after the initial leptospiral infection, the patient developed progressive behavioral and psychiatric abnormalities. According to his family, he became increasingly irritable, emotionally unstable, and preoccupied with trivial matters. He exhibited persistent persecutory delusions, believing that his neighbors were encroaching on his land, and reacted with anger when family members attempted to reason with him. Episodes of auditory and visual hallucinations were reported, including hearing indistinct voices and seeing shadow-like figures. His personality gradually changed:he became socially withdrawn, rigid in thinking, and occasionally impulsive, including loudly singing patriotic songs to "protest" perceived injustices. A follow-up brain MRI performed in October 2025 revealed chronic lacunar infarctions in the pons, right thalamus, and bilateral basal ganglia, Fazekas grade 2 white matter degeneration, and a stable arachnoid cyst in the cisterna magna, but no evidence of active inflammation or recurrence. Neurology consultation suggested that his symptoms likely reflected a combination of post-meningitic neuropsychiatric sequelae and emotional dysregulation rather than a primary psychiatric disorder.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 60-year-old male presenting with a 3-day history of fever, chills, vomiting, and recurrent convulsions.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Symptoms began 3 days prior to admission with abrupt fever and chills peaking at 40 °C, which failed to improve with over-the-counter cold medications. On the second day of illness, he developed recurrent generalized seizures accompanied by vomiting of gastric contents, followed by progressive deterioration of consciousness leading to emergency hospital admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical history, no regular medications, no known drug allergies. No personal or family history of psychiatric illness. Occupation: farmer living in a rural area of Jiangxi province, China.
subjective.review_of_systems: Reports acute fever, shaking chills, nausea, vomiting of gastric contents, recurrent generalized seizures, and altered level of consciousness. Home medications: over-the-counter cold medication. Allergies: no known drug allergies.

objective.physical_examination: Upon admission: body temperature 37.2 °C (febrile peak 40 °C prior to admission), regular heart rate 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, blood pressure 131/76 mmHg. Chest: clear to auscultation anteriorly. Neurological: altered consciousness, increased generalized muscle tone, mild neck stiffness; negative Brudzinski and Kernig signs.
objective.routine_investigations: Inflammatory markers: procalcitonin markedly elevated at 27.68 ng/mL (ref 0-0.05), heparin-binding protein 75 ng/mL (ref 0-15), C-reactive protein 69.45 mg/L (ref 0-8). Complete blood count: white blood cell count 6.46 x 10^9/L, platelet count decreased at 87 x 10^9/L. Liver and renal panel: alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 128.7 U/L (ref 9-50), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 115.2 U/L (ref 15-40), serum creatinine 101.8 mcmol/L (ref 57-97). COVID-19 RT-PCR: negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Lumbar puncture: cerebrospinal fluid WBC count 1/mcL (ref 0-10), protein elevated at 1038 mg/L (ref 150-450), glucose 3.18 mmol/L (ref 2.8-4.4). Chest CT: diffuse ground-glass opacities and patchy consolidations in bilateral lungs; follow-up CT demonstrated marked radiographic resolution of pulmonary infiltrates. Brain MRI: multiple, mildly asymmetric lesions with slightly prolonged T1 and T2 signals involving bilateral parietal lobes, centrum semiovale, bilateral thalami, brainstem, and bilateral cerebellum; slightly hyperintense on DWI and FLAIR without significant contrast enhancement, consistent with inflammatory lesions; 2-week follow-up MRI showed marked lesion regression; 3-year follow-up MRI showed chronic lacunar infarctions (pons, right thalamus, basal ganglia), Fazekas grade 2 white matter degeneration, and stable cisterna magna arachnoid cyst without active inflammation.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Leptospiral meningoencephalitis with diffuse inflammatory CNS lesions, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, acute hepatitis, and thrombocytopenia, definitively confirmed by cerebrospinal fluid metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) positive for Leptospira. Ruled out COVID-19 infection. Long-term course was complicated 3 years later by post-meningitic neuropsychiatric sequelae (persecutory delusions, auditory and visual hallucinations, irritability, emotional dysregulation, and personality change) rather than a primary psychiatric illness.
Plan & Treatment: Initial empiric antimicrobial coverage with intravenous vancomycin (1000 mg q12h) and intravenous meropenem (1000 mg q8h), de-escalated to targeted intravenous penicillin sodium (40 WU q8h) following mNGS pathogen confirmation. Supportive anticonvulsant and neurologic care; outpatient neuropsychiatric evaluation and supportive management for late sequelae.
Outcome: Acute clinical and radiographic resolution within two weeks, with marked clearance of pulmonary infiltrates and brain lesions; late development of post-encephalitic behavioral and psychiatric symptoms at three years.
